profile.campus: Lumen / Level 3 Texas Triangle (Dallas / Austin / San Antonio)
profile.reading:
This Lumen colocation facility, internally identified in public records as Dallas 6, is located at 1150 Regal Row, Dallas, TX 75247, a separate building from the nearby Irving Boulevard Lumen Dallas facility also tracked in this registry; Lumen does not publish individual building addresses or specs on its own site for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites. Lumen Technologies, formerly CenturyLink (renamed Lumen on September 14, 2020, with its stock ticker changing from CTL to LUMN on September 18, 2020) and built in part on CenturyLink's November 1, 2017 acquisition of Level 3 Communications, operates this facility as part of a network-centric edge colocation product rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen's own colocation data sheet states more than 175 carrier-neutral data centers across more than 60 North American markets, offering cabinet power in the 3 to 15 kilowatt range described as varying by site; unlike the wholesale operators tracked elsewhere in this registry, Lumen does not disclose per-building square footage or total MW capacity for any of its sites.

Texas's data center sales tax exemption cost the state roughly $5-30 million a year from 2014 through 2022, jumped to more than $150 million in 2023, and is now projected at $1.3 billion for the current fiscal year, $3.2 billion over 2026-2028, and nearly $1.8 billion annually by fiscal 2030, according to the Texas Tribune. Separately, ERCOT's interconnection queue holds roughly 474 gigawatts of pending requests, more than five times the grid's record peak demand, with Governor Abbott stating about 90% of new power requests are data centers; Abbott ordered an audit of queued data centers in August 2026, and ERCOT sought a delay of its transmission planning study from the Public Utility Commission the same month.

reading.body:
Lumen Dallas 6 is a carrier-neutral colocation facility at 1150 Regal Row in Dallas, operated by Lumen Technologies as part of a network-centric edge product rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen does not publish per-building capacity, square footage, or certifications for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites, only a general cabinet power range of 3 to 15 kilowatts varying by location. No IT load figure, rack count, or power delivery specification is available from the operator.

Texas holds 133 mapped data center facilities of which only 18 have published megawatt figures totaling 468 MW. This campus cannot be ranked among those 18 because its capacity is unpublished. The state's data center tax exemption cost ballooned from roughly $5-30 million annually through 2022 to a projected $1.3 billion for fiscal 2026 and nearly $1.8 billion by 2030. ERCOT's interconnection queue now holds roughly 474 gigawatts of pending requests, more than five times record peak demand, with Governor Abbott stating about 90 percent of new power requests are data centers.

Without published capacity, this facility cannot be weighed against the grid constraint that now binds AI scaling in Texas. Lumen's business model is edge colocation for carriers and enterprises in small cabinet densities, not hyperscale AI training infrastructure. Whether this campus matters to AI depends on whether Lumen intends to offer higher-density power delivery than its published 3-15 kilowatt cabinet specification, a fact the operator has not disclosed.
